answer.label: Not Will Rogers — an unsourced modern maxim
answer.authorName: Unknown — falsely credited to Will Rogers
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · absent from Rogers’s complete 1922–1935 newspaper columns
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Will Rogers ever said or wrote this. Wikiquote files the line in the Misattributed section of its Will Rogers page, with no citation, and we found no instance of it in the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s own free online editions of his complete syndicated output — the six volumes of Weekly Articles (1922–1935) and the four-volume Daily Telegrams set (1926–1935), roughly 1.4 million words, searched in full. The same sentence also circulates as a John Wooden coaching maxim, but that credit is equally unsourced: no first publication has ever been documented for either man.

source.excerpt: Don’t let yesterday use up too much of today.
trail: Anchor: Wikiquote lists “Don't let yesterday use up too much of today.” in the Misattributed section of its Will Rogers page, with no supporting citation.

Primary check: we downloaded and searched the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s free online editions of his complete syndicated output — Weekly Articles in six volumes (1922–1935) and the complete four-volume Daily Telegrams set, running to his last column of 12 August 1935. That is roughly 1.4 million words, and it contains no instance of the phrase or any near variant. (His six books and magazine pieces are not part of these volumes.)
The museum’s curated Will’s Quotes page does not include the line, and carries the notice that “Some quotes attributed to Will Rogers are falsely credited,” with contact details for its curator.

The same sentence is presented as a John Wooden maxim on TheWoodenEffect.com — produced by SUCCESS magazine with the John R. Wooden family — and in Wooden’s Wisdom, but neither supplies a book, speech or date, so that credit rests on no firmer footing than the Rogers one.
source.excerptNote: There is no original context to quote. The sentence circulates only as a standalone motivational line, with no located column, speech, book or date behind it — and in two competing wordings, “use up” and “take up.”
source.rightsNote: Because no first publication has ever been identified for this sentence, its copyright status cannot be determined, and no public-domain claim should be made for it. Had it genuinely been Rogers’s it would very likely be public domain — his columns ran from 1922 to August 1935, much of that output published before 1931 — but the line is absent from those columns, and the competing John Wooden credit would point instead to a much later, still-in-copyright text.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: About Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, newspaper columnist & film star
author.bio: Will Rogers was born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation near Oologah, Indian Territory, and rose from trick roping to the Ziegfeld Follies, to Hollywood, and to a syndicated newspaper column that ran from 1922 until his death in an Alaska plane crash on 15 August 1935. His weekly articles and daily telegrams made him one of the most widely read commentators in America. That plainspoken, wry, endlessly quotable voice is precisely why unsourced aphorisms keep landing under his name — and why the museum that keeps his papers has to warn readers that some of them are false.

misattribution.heading: How the misattribution works
misattribution.intro: This is a floating motivational one-liner with two famous homes and no documented parent. Both credits are assertion rather than evidence, and the wording is not even stable between them.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line in the Misattributed section of its Will Rogers page, with no citation. Quote databases carry it under his name with no source at all — Goodreads hosts it while noting that its quotes are added by the community and are not verified.

We searched the Will Rogers Memorial Museum’s free online editions of the complete Weekly Articles (six volumes, 1922–1935) and the complete four-volume Daily Telegrams set (1926–1935) — roughly 1.4 million words — and the phrase does not occur in any form. The museum’s own curated Will’s Quotes page does not carry it either, and states that “Some quotes attributed to Will Rogers are falsely credited.”

The identical sentence is promoted as a maxim of the UCLA basketball coach on TheWoodenEffect.com, produced by SUCCESS magazine in cooperation with the John R. Wooden family, and in the Wooden’s Wisdom newsletter. Neither names a book, speech or date, so Wooden is best described as a prominent user of the line, not a documented author of it.

“Use up” and “take up” both circulate under Rogers’s name — Goodreads hosts the ‘use up’ and ‘take up’ forms as two separate Rogers entries. Unstable wording with no source text behind it is a standard signature of an orphan quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: not Will Rogers. Wikiquote files it as misattributed, and it appears nowhere in his complete published columns. Whoever wrote it has never been identified.

context.heading: Why it lands on Will Rogers
lead: Rogers is one of the safest-looking places in American English to park an orphan aphorism. He wrote in short, plain, self-contained sentences; he published so much — over 3,600 newspaper columns in sixteen years, by the museum’s count — that almost any homespun line feels like it could be in there somewhere; and he died in 1935, long enough ago that nobody expects to be handed a page number.

The tell here is that the sentence has no fixed form. It travels as “don’t let yesterday use up too much of today” and as “don’t let yesterday take up too much of today,” both filed under Rogers on the same quote sites. Genuine quotations tend to stabilise around the text that was actually printed. Wording that keeps sliding is usually wording that was never printed anywhere in particular.
context.detailsSummary: What “not in Rogers” actually means here
detailsBody: The Will Rogers Memorial Museums have put his syndicated journalism online as free PDFs: Weekly Articles in six volumes covering 1922 to 1935, and a complete four-volume set of the Daily Telegrams running from 1926 to his final column of 12 August 1935. Together that is roughly 1.4 million words — effectively the whole of the writing that made him a household name.

Searching that text for the phrase, and for its component fragments, returns nothing. This is a strong negative but not a total one: Rogers also published six books and a run of magazine pieces, which are not in those volumes, and he spoke constantly on stage and radio without transcripts. So the honest verdict is that the line is absent from his published columns and undocumented everywhere else — not that its non-existence has been proved.

The John Wooden trail is worth following and stops just as quickly. Wooden was famous for exactly this kind of compressed maxim, and the line is presented as his on sites made with his family’s cooperation — but none of them names a book, a talk or a year, which is what would be needed to call him the author rather than a very effective repeater.
context.pull: A real quote has a page it came from. This one has two spellings, two famous names, and no page.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Will Rogers page lists "Don't let yesterday use up too much of today." in its Misattributed section, with no citation.
The Will Rogers Memorial Museum's Will's Quotes page states "Some quotes attributed to Will Rogers are falsely credited" and gives curator contact details; the line does not appear on the page.

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum hosts free downloadable PDF editions of Rogers's Weekly Articles (6 volumes) and Daily Telegrams, and states he published approximately two million words — six books and over 3,600 newspaper columns — from 1916 to August 1935. The PDFs served from this page are Weekly Articles vols. 1–6 (1922–1935) and the complete 4-volume Daily Telegrams set (1926–1935); a full-text search of them for the phrase and its fragments returns zero matches across ~1.45 million words.
Goodreads carries "Don't let yesterday use up too much of today." credited to Will Rogers with no book or source citation, and notes that quotes are added by the community and not verified.
The variant "Don't let yesterday take up too much of today" is separately hosted on Goodreads, also credited to Will Rogers with no source.

TheWoodenEffect.com — produced by SUCCESS magazine in cooperation with the John R. Wooden family — lists "Don't let yesterday take up too much of today." as a John Wooden quote, with no source citation.
Wooden's Wisdom Issue 56 presents "Don't let yesterday take up too much of today" as a foundational Coach John Wooden maxim and quotes his explanation of the idea.

Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 near Oologah, Indian Territory, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation; performed in vaudeville and the Ziegfeld Follies; acted in film; wrote a syndicated newspaper column from 1922 to 1935 (daily from 1926); and died in a plane crash in Alaska on 15 August 1935.
John Wooden (14 October 1910 – 4 June 2010) was UCLA's head basketball coach 1948–1975, won 10 NCAA championships, and was known for short motivational messages and his 'Pyramid of Success'.
Quote Investigator's site search returns no article for this phrase — QI has not investigated it, so there is no QI anchor finding to defer to.
